system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2160-08-18 19:26:00 to 2160-08-21 16:54:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a man with a history of coronary artery disease and prior stent placement, was admitted for escalating chest pain radiating to the neck and jaw, accompanied by dyspnea, sweating, and nausea. He had not been taking his cardiac medications, including Plavix and aspirin, for about a month. Initial evaluation showed no acute heart attack, but an echocardiogram revealed new regional wall motion abnormalities, raising concern for possible stent occlusion. His pain resolved with medical therapy. During admission, he disclosed ongoing heroin use and experienced withdrawal symptoms, for which he received clonidine and Ativan. Despite recommendations to remain for detox placement, he chose to self-discharge to seek treatment independently. He was discharged home with a full medication refill, follow-up instructions, and referrals for addiction and housing support.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery

blockages. We found that you did not have any blockages. This 
means that the chest pain you are having is probably not from 
your heart. You should follow up with your primary care doctor 
as scheduled to evaluate for other causes of your chest pain. 
You should continue to take all of your medications. This will 
help to prevent future problems with your heart. You should also 
follow up with your cardiologist as intructed.

We did not make any changes to your medications.

Thank you for coming to the ___ 
___. It was a pleasure taking care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You came in tonight with chest pain. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, doc. This morning I had sharp chest pain again, like last time. It went up to my neck, down my arm, and into my back. It wasn’t from moving or walking—it just came on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you have any shortness of breath, sweating, or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Shortness of breath, yeah—I’ve had that for about a month. But no nausea or sweating this time. I also had fevers and chills for a few days before the pain came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned going to another hospital recently. What did they say?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said I might have pneumonia or a COPD flare-up. Gave me antibiotics and prednisone, but I didn’t fill the script. Felt a little better, but the fevers didn’t go away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve checked your EKG and blood work. Your troponin—heart damage marker—was normal. But your EKG shows old changes, like from a past heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… is my heart okay? I was worried after last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, we don’t see signs of a new heart attack. But because of your history—stents, missed medications—we started you on a heparin drip just in case. We’ll keep an eye on your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped taking Plavix and aspirin last time because I didn’t have money for meds. I know it was dumb.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Not taking those increases your risk. But we’re going to help you stay on track this time. We’ll refill everything before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray came back—no pneumonia or fluid. Lungs look clear. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So it’s not my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Doesn’t look like it. We also did blood cultures to check for infection—those came back negative. No sign of sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat troponins are still negative. That means no new heart muscle damage. We’ve stopped the heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not having a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not right now. But we want to be sure. You’ll have a stress test today—a nuclear imaging study—to check for blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s safe. You’ll walk on a treadmill, and we’ll take pictures of your heart. Even with your prior EKG changes, the imaging will show if blood flow is reduced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back from the stress test. Good news—you exercised well, no chest pain. The images show no new blockages in your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain wasn’t from my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. It’s called atypical chest pain—could be musculoskeletal, nerve-related, or from stress. But your heart is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling anxious, sweating a lot, and my stomach’s been off since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I think that’s withdrawal. You mentioned heroin use before. These symptoms—sweating, anxiety, diarrhea—are common when stopping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I’ve been trying to quit. It’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can help. We’ll start clonidine and diazepam to ease the symptoms. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling tonight? Any better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the shaking’s gone. Sweating less. Still anxious, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep the meds for a few days and taper them off. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count was high when you came in—12.9—but it’s now down to 8.5. That means no active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the fevers were from withdrawal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Withdrawal can cause fevers and chills. Or it could’ve been a mild viral illness. Either way, you’re improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doc, I live with my brother. He used heroin too, but he’s clean now. I want to stay clean too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Support helps. We’ll refer you to a support group and addiction counseling. You’ve already taken the hardest step—wanting to change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready to go home today. Your pain’s gone, no heart issues, and withdrawal symptoms are under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are my meds the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. We’re keeping your aspirin, Plavix, metoprolol, lisinopril, and citalopram. We lowered your pravastatin dose due to liver values, but it’s still protective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the clonazepam?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue that for anxiety as prescribed. But please don’t stop any meds again—even if you feel fine. They prevent heart problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Follow up with your primary doctor and cardiologist. And please consider the addiction support—we want you to stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks, doc. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes—especially chest pain or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. The nurse will give you your prescriptions and instructions.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with atypical chest pain radiating to the neck, arm, and back, following a recent hospitalization for similar symptoms. He had stopped cardiac medications previously, raising concern for stent thrombosis, but serial troponins were negative and a stress test showed no new blockages. Initial fevers and leukocytosis resolved without evidence of infection. He developed opiate withdrawal symptoms during admission, which were managed with clonidine and diazepam. His symptoms improved, and he expressed motivation to remain abstinent from opioids. He was discharged home with continued cardiac medications, referrals for addiction support, and follow-up plans.
